claims.text: Integrating DFT with machine-learning corrections can accurately predict low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys.
The integrated approach will improve predictive accuracy by at least 20% over current predictions.
Machine-learning models can account for the lattice distortions and disorder characteristic of high-entropy alloys.
Lattice distortions and disorder scatter phonons and reduce thermal conductivity.
The target materials are solid high-entropy alloys with FCC or BCC crystal structures.
The target alloys contain multiple principal elements in near-equal proportions.
The calculations will use supercells of at least 4x4x4 unit cells.
The calculations will use a 10x10x10 k-point mesh.
The machine-learning model will be trained on at least 1000 high-entropy-alloy structures.
Samples will be produced by arc melting or mechanical alloying and annealed at 1000 °C for 24 hours.
Room-temperature thermal conductivity will be measured by the laser-flash method.
Machine-learning corrections account for anharmonic effects and lattice vibrations not captured by traditional DFT methods.
Accounting for those anharmonic effects and lattice vibrations improves predictions of phonon thermal conductivity.
The approach will predict phonon thermal conductivity values at least 20% lower than current predictions.
The identified alloys will have room-temperature thermal conductivity below 4 W/m-K.
Traditional DFT methods or empirical models currently have an average predictive accuracy of 80%.
The approach is applicable only to high-entropy alloys containing 3-5 principal elements.
The approach is limited to FCC or BCC structures that can be modeled accurately with DFT and machine-learning corrections.
The hypothesis is falsified if prediction errors exceed 12% for at least 85% of tested samples.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis defines the claimed 20% improvement as an increase in predictive accuracy, whereas the predicted outcome defines it as a 20% reduction in the predicted conductivity value. These are different metrics and are not interchangeable.

The central claim is superiority over an 80%-accurate baseline, but the falsification rule tests only absolute prediction error and does not compare the proposed approach with the stated baseline. It therefore cannot decisively test the claimed improvement over current predictions.
